speakeroldname: Hon. C. M. Drury (Minister of Industry):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: MR. DRURY-CORRECTION OF ANSWER RESPECTING MOTOR CAR PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday during an exchange on the orders of the day a question was asked of me in relation to motor car prices, and I misunderstood the question. I had understood, in the background noise, that I was being asked whether I had said during the election campaign that there would be parity of car prices in Canada and the United States, to which my answer was no.
On reading Hansard I found that the question, as reported at page 282 of Hansard, was:
Did the minister not make an announcement during the election campaign to the effect that the price of Canadian cars had been reduced?
Of course, Mr. Speaker, the answer to that question is "Yes". An announcement was made in late October, on October 28, pointing out that announcements by Canadian automobile manufacturers respecting 1966 models indicated that in relation to similarly equipped 1965 model cars, there were reductions in prices. I do not want to have misled the house. There were reductions in car prices compared to similarly equipped 1965 model cars, and I did make an announcement in October last to that effect.

subtopic: MR. DRURY-CORRECTION OF ANSWER RESPECTING MOTOR CAR PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was going to rise on a question of privilege in connection with the same matter, but the minister has answered it. However, if it is permissible I should like to make some further remarks about what he has said in answer to my question, and to state that the minister also said in the city of Kitchener on October 26, as reported in the Ottawa Citizen:
Industry Minister Drury said Tuesday night the Canada-United States automobile agreement will save Canadian car buyers about $49,000,000 this year.
Mr. Drury estimated that prices have dropped an average of $70 on each car and, with about 700,000 cars expected to be sold in Canada this year, that makes a saving to buyers of about $49,000,000.
"I suggest to you that the agreement is not only working but is working in the right direction," he told about 200 persons at a Liberal rally.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

speechtext: The house resumed, from Wednesday, January 26, consideration of the motion of Mr. Goyer for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Lambert.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at six o'clock yesterday evening I was interrupted by the clock. I was making a plea for some attention to be paid by the present administration to the problems facing Canadian agriculture. It would take years to go through the list of what has been neglected in this regard.
The Speech from the Throne debate is our one opportunity to cover most of the subjects which are of interest to a backbencher in bringing forward the needs of his constituents. I was extremely disappointed by the fact that I was unable to do very much about my election promise in the matter of old age pensions, but since we have completed the debate on that subject I will pass on to what I regard as another most important matter.
We are continually hearing from all sides of the house of the need for reform in parliament and streamlining our procedures. The Leader of the Opposition has often been blamed, except by his own party, for not allowing the work of the house to proceed. I have done some research on the subject, and I find that the present Leader of the Official

January 27, 1966
The Address-Mr. Bigg Opposition has always been foremost in meeting reasonable requirements in this field but has not been given the credit for the lead he has always taken in this regard. I might mention the question of speaking time in the house and the restriction which was imposed,
I think quite rightly, limiting members to 40 minutes. We have always been and always will be, I trust, willing to put our weight behind any reasonable reforms in our procedure.
I hasten to say, however, that I do not think there is any need for tremendous changes in our rules, though perhaps at times we need some changes in our individual attitudes. I do not think a rule book can ever be a proper check. No strait-jacketing of the rights and privileges of members can ever hasten our march toward a bigger and better Canada. I would resist any encroachment upon the rules we have because I think these rules are quite adequate for most purposes.
I see in the Speech from the Throne that the government is promising equality of opportunity for everybody in Canada. Today I want to speak for our first citizens in Canada, the Indians, and express the hope that this administration will put the formation of an Indian claims commission high on the list of priorities. I believe the Indians have always been willing to take their place as citizens of Canada and put forth the necessary effort. For many years the Indian affairs branch has taken a paternalistic approach. We have thrown up our hands and said nothing can be done for the Indians. I say that the best possible thing we can do for the Indians is to proceed as rapidly as possible to make them entirely self-sufficient.
The Indians do not want relief. They do not want welfare. They merely want an opportunity to upgrade themselves and play a full part in the development of this country, a country which at one time was theirs. They have lived up to their part of the agreements in the treaties. I do not think we have done so. The earlier we bring forward this claims commission and clear up once and for all whether we have kept our promises as set out in these treaties, and go back as far as we can to restore to these people their dignity and their right to live in Canada as free and equal citizens, the better it will be.
One step in this direction would, I am sure, be the appointment as soon as possible of at least a deputy minister of Indian affairs of Indian origin. The Indian people do not trust the white man in this country, and I do not

see any reason so far why they should. They will never have complete confidence in any Indian affairs branch until they are directly represented by somebody of their own blood and of their own choosing.
[DOT] (12:00 noon)
There is one tremendous danger in the bill which has already been proposed concerning Indian affairs and the setting up of an Indian commission. It is suggested that the government should have the right to remove the Indian representative on the commission through a joint address to both houses of parliament. I do not care how it is hedged around; any government that tried to exercise that right would do nothing less than completely destroy any good which such a commission could hope to perform. I for one will vigorously oppose any restriction on the rights of our native people to speak freely at all times and have a representative of their own choice put forward their side of a claim.
We have got past the point where any kind of official rubberstamp, no matter how well intended, can adequately represent the needs of these people. It was the pride of our administration when we were in power that we gave the Indians the long promised ballot. Many of the native people were afraid that using the ballot would militate against their rights but now they are becoming used to it and see in it a real hope that they will be able to take their full part in Canadian affairs.
There is to be a new adjustment of the Indian affairs department. I would like to see at the same time an examination of our national parks administration. As a nature lover I would be the last to restrict in any way the preservation of our natural beauty and natural life, but I am certain there was a dual purpose in setting up the national parks, the second being to make sure there were adequate recreational facilities to permit our people to enjoy the natural beauty which our forefathers took the trouble to lay aside.
The Wood Buffalo park in northern Alberta is an area of 17,500 squares miles, rich in minerals and natural resources, but largely wasted. It is not a recreational park in any way, shape or form. It is true we have a large herd of buffalo in it, and 30 or 40 whooping cranes, but we do not need 17,500 square miles of land to look after that small amount of wildlife.
A year or two ago I took it upon myself to help open negotiations with the provincial government of Alberta to see if we could take
January 27, 1966

a new look at the whole question of national parks, always with the aim of preserving the natural beauty and wildlife of northern Alberta. The same principle should be used in the rest of Canada when we decide to take a good look at national parks and see whether many of the resources of our country might not better be spent in areas further south which are more beautiful, more accessible and more useful for the secondary purpose of recreation, which may in effect be the primary purpose of national parks in promoting the health and recreation of our people.
So far we have had absolutely no co-operation from the provincial government of Alberta. The premier of Alberta, Mr. Manning, has said he cannot get co-operation from the federal members of parliament in matters such as this. However, it has been my personal experience, which I believe is shared by other federal M.P.'s that the door is locked from the provincial side and certainly not from the federal side. When I was trying to have these negotiations started I got the full co-operation of the Prime Minister and of the minister of northern affairs, who at that time had responsibility for national parks. There was a wide open door policy so far as discussions were concerned. We made no foolish promises except to say "Let's get together and talk it over." The door has been opened on the federal side. Unless it is opened from the other side these false accusations concerning co-operation should cease.
I am interested to note in the Speech from the Throne that the administration is interested in the affairs of youth, but I do not think the promises in the speech go nearly far enough. In this last half of the twentieth century the proper training of youth, both with regard to higher education and trade education, and the question of their physical welfare are so important that it is high time we set up a full ministry-call it the ministry of youth, call it the ministry of federal education, call it what you will-to take care of this whole matter.
I have some very definite views on this subject. One that leaps to my mind is that steps should be taken to try to standardize education across Canada. We talk about equality of opportunity, but we find many cases where children spend years in high school, then when they move from one province to another they lose a whole year out of their academic life, and sometimes two, so that the left hand does not know what the right hand is doing. We do not want to carry
The Address-Mr. Bigg on toward the end of this century in a haphazard manner, in the matter of training our youth either in physical or mental standards.
It is my sincere hope that the government will take a new look at the idea of a corps of youth, make it a complete national project, and give it the full status it deserves with a minister of the crown in charge, a minister who can bring together all these varied and difficult problems under one effective department in order that we can give proper attention to our young people.
I also note that something is going to be done with regard to consolidating pension rights in the civil service. I expect this will also include the R.C.M.P. and the armed forces. This is an opportunity for the government to get out of what I think is a rather sticky situation with regard to pension schemes. Perhaps with adequate adjustments to the existing pension schemes we can plug some of the holes in what I consider to be the inadequate pension scheme we passed last session. This would also be a timely opportunity to revise the pension schemes of those people who spent most of their lives in the public service and who are now retired, the veterans of the civil service who in some cases are trying to get along on a pitiful allowance. Many of them are receiving less than $100 a month after a lifetime of service.
It is not a good enough excuse to offer, as we did with regard to some of the other federal statutes we passed recently, that we do not know where the money is coming from; because when the whim of the government is such that it wants to spend money in large and unlimited quantities, no apology whatsoever is made to the taxpayers of Canada. We can find scores of millions of dollars for such luxuries as the C.B.C. and centennial grants. I do not say these are not worthy causes, but I do think that paying adequate pensions to the veterans of the civil service, the armed forces and the R.C.M.P. is far more important and should have priority over the fringe benefits of culture and the expensive commissions of one form or another that we set up to see that the luxury side of our life is looked after properly.
[DOT] (12:10 p.m.)
It is high time we co-ordinated our efforts in this regard and put first things first. I would place at the top of the list the rewarding of those people who have already given the productive years of their lives to the betterment of Canada and its people. I said

January 27, 1966
Division
last night, and I repeat, that there is no excuse for the government in the fact that it is a minority government, because a minority government in 1957 launched Canada on a very progressive, imaginative and courageous program, the like of which has not been seen since.
We are criticized almost daily for criticizing the government, but what is the main function of the opposition? I suggest our main function is to keep the government on the rails. It is not our job to run around backslapping them. The government will receive that sort of praise and appreciation in this country when it performs well. If it does not perform well it is our plain duty to offer constructive criticism. I think some members on the other side of the house will be the first to admit that during the past three years, had it not been for constructive criticism from this side of the house, Canada might well now be in a very serious state.
I am not one to cry the blues. Canada at this time is experiencing a tremendous boom. I demand that the products of that boom period be not wasted, and that the high production and wealth which Canada now enjoys be adequately distributed to those people who deserve it. To do so would not require an adoption of socialism in Canada. There are many things which even a Liberal administration might do without looking to that corner of the house for the support they might find elsewhere. The government will always receive the support of the official opposition at any time it brings forward constructive programs for the welfare of this country. We in the official opposition do not put the party first we put Canada first. That is why I am pleased to see our team strengthened. We have a fine group of recruits, and we welcome back to the front benches those men who made such a magnificent contribution when they were sitting on the treasury benches.
Mr. Speaker, let me warn the Liberal party at this time that we intend to turn out on many more occasions at 100 per cent strength, as we did the other night. We are not only going to be watchdogs; we are going to be workhorses.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at one o'clock I was about to begin my remarks on the main subject on which I intend to speak for a few minutes this afternoon, namely, financial relations between Canada and the United States and the implications of some of the

Hon. members will recall that for more than a decade Canada has been spending more abroad than it has been earning abroad. The deficit has been as high as $1J billion in 1959. In 1963 and 1964 it was down to about half a billion dollars. In 1965 it got up to about $1 billion and during the present year it will probably be a little more.
At times of prosperity like the present when our own resources are almost fully employed, this current account deficit and the import of capital which accompanies it enables us to grow and develop more rapidly than would otherwise have been the case. We are, of course, able to have these continuing substantial deficits only because we are able to finance them.
Where is this capital to come from? Only from the United States can we expect to raise private long term capital in the quantities that are required to finance this substantial and continuing excess of current international payments over current international receipts. Neither the volume of saving disposed toward foreign investment nor the organization of the capital markets is great enough in Europe or elsewhere to supply more than a modest fraction of our requirements. We are fortunate that for a variety of reasons Canada enjoys the confidence of American investors. It is that confidence which enables us to invest and to grow at the high rates that we desire, and indeed expect, while also maintaining a high standard of consumption.
There are differences of view whether it is desirable that we should incur such substantial current account deficits year after year and import capital on the scale that we do. One point, however, is obvious, namely, that it makes more sense to incur deficits and import such large sums of capital at a time when we are working close to potential and growing rapidly, as is now the case, than it was, say, in 1959 when the party opposite was in power and there was a high rate of unemployment. I have already mentioned the figure for 1959 when Canada was in a bit of a recession. That year we were importing capital at the rate of a billion and a half dollars a year. It is none the less true that we are heavily dependent upon being able to import the capital we need and we are therefore vulnerable to any change in the United States capital markets or any restrictions placed on the United States capital markets of a nature
January 27, 1966	COMMONS
that would interfere with the flow of capital into Canada.
This leads one immediately to consider the position of the United States today. It is hard for us, living as we do just across the border and perhaps even more difficult for people living at a greater distance from the United States, to realize that a country as powerful and as rich as the United States, one whose currency is in such demand in so many parts of the world, can have a balance of payments problem. Yet there is no doubt that it has. although it is very different from ours.
Unlike Canada, the United States normally has a large surplus on its current international account. That is to say its earnings abroad exceed its spendings abroad. The amount of the surplus varies of course from year to year, but the general pattern is clear and strong.
The problem of the United States arises from the fact that the American people and the American government, for one reason or another, have in recent years wished to invest abroad, provide as foreign aid, or utilize for defence purposes much more each year than was available from the surplus in their current account balance of payments.
The flow of private investment from the United States has been running at billions of dollars a year for many years. It has contributed in the short run to the over-all deficit in the balance of payments which the United States has experienced. These over-all deficits show up in the loss of the United States gold reserves and in the accumulation of claims on the United States by central banks and governments of other countries and by other banks. While some of us, such as Canada, are only too glad to hold most of our exchange reserves in the form of United States balances and short term investments, others have been accumulating more of such reserves in U.S. dollars than they feel they would really like to hold and they wish from time to time to convert substantial amounts of such balances into gold, thereby reducing the ultimate reserves into which the U.S. dollars are convertible. For the past several years the United States government has been taking measures to deal with the situation. The more important and spectacular of these measures have been those which aim at reducing the flow of U.S. investments to other countries.
From what I have said earlier about Canada's position, it is evident that we are particularly vulnerable to restrictions on the
DEBATES	323
The Address-Mr. Sharp outflow of U.S. capital. At first sight it might look as if we were the country most seriously affected. In fact, however, the United States cannot really improve its own balance of payments situation by restricting the flow of capital to Canada. That is the difference between the Canadian position and the position of other countries. In short, we are not a drain on the United States. We provide support to the U.S. balance of payments.
One of the first important measures the United States took to improve its balance of payments was the interest equalization tax, a tax payable by United States investors on the purchases of foreign securities. This was intended to make foreign investment less attractive to Americans. When this was first announced by President Kennedy in July, 1963, there was consternation in the financial markets of Canada because it was quickly realized that this measure as originally proposed would either leave Canada seriously short of foreign exchange and investment capital or would necessitate a substantial increase in interest rates in Canada to levels that would induce Canadian borrower -provinces, municipalities and corporations -to borrow in the United States in the required volume despite the tax, and I would suggest the order of magnitude is more than a 1 per cent increase in interest rates which, under these circumstances, is very substantial.
Fortunately we were quickly able to convince Mr. Dillon, then Secretary of the Treasury, and through him President Kennedy, that for the reasons I have described it was not possible for the United States to improve its balance of payments position by reducing the exports of capital to Canada below what was required to meet Canada's current account deficit. Consequently, the United States authorities agreed to exempt new issues of Canadian securities from the interest equalization tax. In return, the Canadian government undertook that it was not its intention to increase its foreign exchange reserves through the proceeds of borrowing in the United States.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
For some months after the announcement of this special interest equalization tax in the United States there was uncertainty as to just how it would apply and the need for working out specific aspects of the exemption. During this period there were relatively few issues of Canadian securities in the United States. Once the situation had clarified, however,
January 27, 1966

The Address-Mr. Sharp U.S. lenders and Canadian borrowers anticipated the final enactment of the law and the exemption, both of which were to be retroactive, and a big backlog of Canadian issues held up during the months of uncertainty moved on to the U.S. market in the second, third and fourth quarters of 1964. In keeping with the spirit of our undertaking to the United States, the former minister of finance, my predecessor in office, appealed to the provincial authorities in December, 1964, to avoid as far as possible adding to the volume of new Canadian issues in the United States at that time.
Early in 1965 President Johnson reinforced the interest equalization tax with a program of "guidelines"-advice, suggestions-for voluntary action on the part of U.S. investors and companies to restrain the flow of their investment outside the United States and bring back to the United States such funds as they reasonably could which had been held abroad by them or their subsidiaries. These guidelines made in February contained some specific provisions for Canada in keeping with the special circumstances which had been recognized in the exemption granted Canadian issues from the interest equalization tax. Notwithstanding these provisions, however, the guidelines of early 1965 did cause some difficulties in the Canadian market for short term securities which did not benefit from the special provisions applicable to long term investment.
I now come to more recent events in respect of which I think this house is particularly interested. In the latter part of 1965, at a season when the Canadian balance of payments is normally relatively strong, our current account and general balance of payments were suddenly strengthened as a result of the second large wheat sale to Russia. During the autumn Canadian borrowers were also selling a large volume of Canadian securities in the United States. As a result, Canada's exchange reserves, including our net . creditor position in the international monetary fund, which is proper to count in this connection, increased well above the level at which we were aiming to hold them in accordance with our understanding with the United States in 1963. We regarded this abnormal rise in our reserves as temporary. I said at the time and I say again, we can reasonably expect to see it reverse in the first half of 1966, but it coincided with a period when the United States was quite concerned over its balance of payments.


The Minister of Finance in November last requested all major Canadian issuers of securities in the United States to defer delivery of their issues, wherever possible, until after the turn of the year when our current account position would be seasonally weaker and the U.S. position could be expected to be stronger. I should like at this time, through the medium of this house, to express the appreciation of the government for the cooperation shown by these Canadian borrowers in meeting this request, and also for the co-operation of the dealers and buyers of the securities concerned.
While a considerable improvement in the United States payments position had resulted from the measures taken in 1963 and from the subsequent guidelines programs instituted by President Johnson last February, the United States over-all deficit remained large and the United States government decided last fall that it must adopt further measures. There were two of these of major concern to Canada.
The first of these was a new guideline, a request by the U.S. authorities to financial institutions other than banks, which includes not only investment companies, insurance companies, etc., but also pension funds and other major buyers of securities, to limit the increase in their holdings of long term foreign investments to a small fraction of their holdings at an earlier date. This was a most important restriction on the sale of long term securities in the United States. It is one that for some reason or other has been overlooked in some of the comment which has been made in the press of this country. If applied to Canada, it would have had very serious adverse effects. We sought and obtained an exemption from this important restriction, justified on the same grounds as our original exemption from the interest equalization tax, and in consideration for an undertaking of the same kind on our part regarding the level of our reserves.
We felt, and when I say "we" I mean the financial authorities in this country-the Bank of Canada and the Department of Finance- that in the present state of the economy it was not desirable to rely too heavily on general monetary and financial measures to control the inflow of capital and a more specific instrument of control might be needed.
I therefore told Mr. Fowler, the Secretary of the Treasury in the United States, when I whs acting minister of finance, that the
January 27, 1966

Canadian government would be prepared, if necessary, to buy outstanding Canadian securities held in the United States to offset any excess flow of U.S. capital to Canada and thus to maintain the net flow of capital at the level required to finance our balance of payments deficit. Instead of adding to U.S. assets in our exchange reserves we would be reducing Canada's liabilities in the United States. Conversely, if the volume of borrowing by other Canadians were not sufficient to meet the balance of payments needs, the government would itself arrange to borrow in the United States. In this way our reserves could be maintained at around the desired level without interfering either with trade or with the normal use of the U.S. long term capital markets by Canadian borrowers. I also agreed that while our reserves must be expected to fluctuate from month to month, we would regard it as appropriate that such fluctuations take place around a level somewhat lower than the mid-1963 figure, say, approximately $2,600 million U.S.
Should it be necessary to borrow in the U.S., I would foresee no great difficulty in obtaining moderate amounts as and when we require them. On the other hand, I believe that there are sufficient government of Canada securities held in the U.S. market to enable us to do what might be required in buying Canadian securities in the U.S. by using the authority to purchase our own securities that is already granted in the Financial Administration Act.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to tell the house that since the beginning of 1966 we have purchased about $40 million worth of our outstanding U.S. bonds that were held in the United States. Our purchase of these securities was consistent with the plan I have outlined but was also intended in considerable part to improve the market for the sale of other Canadian issues in the United States this month when there appeared likely to be a large volume of such issues scheduled for delivery.
The second important measure adopted by the U.S. in December was a voluntary ceiling on direct investment by United States corporations, of whom about 900 will be asked to report regularly on the progress of their co-operation with the United States administration. The guideline, and I will not take time now to give details, does not stipulate how any company shall distribute its direct investment among geographic areas. This is a global restriction. It does not apply to Canada
The Address-Mr. Sharp particularly; it applies to the world. Where it is applied is a matter for the business organization itself to decide. Canada is not exempted from this ceiling or guideline as it was from the previous guideline applying to direct investment.
As soon as we learned of the new United States guidelines for direct investment we told them that while it was very hard for us to assess what its effects on Canada would be because so much depended on the decisions of the businesses, we thought it would cut down some of the flow of such capital to Canada. In so far as it worked in reducing such flow of such capital direct investment it would simply mean a greater need for new issues of Canadian securities in the United States under the arrangements and exemptions provided for long term issues. We felt that from a U.S. point of view there was no reason why the Canadian balance-of-pay-ments deficit with the United States should not be financed by direct investment just as well as by the sale of new issues of securities. Consequently, it seemed to us there was no certainty that the effort to restrict direct investment in Canada would in fact help the U.S. balance of payments at all in the final result.
We also pointed out that the inclusion of retained earnings of subsidiary corporations in the figures used to determine the voluntary quotas for direct investment worked a particular hardship on Canada. U.S. controlled companies form such a large part of Canadian industry and have been so long established in Canada that they must be regarded as a basic and substantial part of the Canadian economy.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
On the basis of these arguments, we suggested that the United States should continue a special exemption for Canada in their guidelines on direct investment or, if they could not see their way clear to do that, they should permit the investment of retained earnings to be outside the quotas.
My understanding is that the American authorities considered the points we put forward, as they said they would, but came to the conclusion that the guideline on direct investment had to be relatively simple and without special exceptions if it was to be effective in meeting the aims of their general program. They did assure us, however, that these guidelines would not affect in any way
326	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Sharp the expansion necessary to achieve the purposes of the Canada-United States automotive agreement.
This guideline on direct investment is intended to restrict the outflow of capital from the United States parent companies to branches and subsidiaries in other countries. There is nothing in these guidelines, so far as I can see-and this is an important point-that would prevent Canadian subsidiaries of United States companies from borrowing like other Canadian companies by means of long term issues in the United States market.
As I said when these guidelines were announced, they have come into effect at a time when capital investment by business in Canada has been increasing very rapidly and cannot be expected to go on increasing at the same rate. In some measure the restraints imposed by the direct investment guidelines will not conflict with the necessities of our own domestic situation. In particular cases they may, however, result in the delay or cancellation of projects that we might have preferred to see proceed. It is our general economic dependence on imported capital which exposes us to dangers of this kind.
In all the circumstances, Mr. Speaker, we have been fortunate in making arrangements that enable us to finance our balance of payments without restriction on current trade or payments and enable us to secure foreign savings to supplement our own.
I cannot agree with those who say that we should have accepted the application of the interest equalization tax and accepted limitations on our right to raise long term funds in the United States and should in return have retained our freedom to increase our reserves at will. As members of this house know, this point of view was urged recently by a man prominent in the financial world. So far as I can see, the result would have been to increase very substantially the cost of Canadians borrowing money both in Canada and the United States without increasing the supply of funds available to us and without gaining anything of substance by way of increased freedom to control our own affairs.
These American guidelines limiting direct investment have also raised another issue, that is to say, whether through them the United States government is interfering in the internal economic affairs of this country. As I have already said, we pointed out to the United States government that this kind of measure as it applied to Canada was of very doubtful value as a means of relieving the

United States balance of payments problem. I believe they would have been better advised to continue the exemption to Canada, both on economic and political grounds. It must be recognized, however, that in attempting to limit the direct investment of its companies abroad the United States government is following well-established precedents. Other countries faced with balance of payments problems-I have in mind, for example, the United Kingdom and France-have taken and do take measures to limit direct investments abroad of their international companies, and I have never never heard any suggestion that either the United Kingdom or France is thereby interfering in the internal affairs of other countries.
I do not like these American guidelines on direct investment and I seriously doubt their wisdom. As a Canadian I find some of the language used by the United States Secretary of the Treasury in appealing to United States companies to co-operate in the program rather objectionable.
But given the over-all arrangements between the Canadian and United States governments which ensure an access to the United States market for long term funds and the scale and nature of the temporary guidelines on direct investment, I do not think there will be damage to the Canadian economy at this time; indeed the results could be advantageous-

It seems to me that I am seeing shades of all the great parliamentarians who came here before us, leaving a deep imprint upon Canadian life. Getting to know certain impressive members of this house constitutes for the new member a challenge to do a little bit more and a little bit better for his constituency, for his province and for his country.
People in some circles wondered why the member for Trois-Rivieres, after having been active within the Liberal party for several years, had decided to run as an independent. At one time, like many other Canadians I realized that the old parties had lost their popular appeal. Mr. Speaker, again as an Independent, I should like to make a suggestion to my colleagues, because there is another state of affairs which did great harm to the old parties. I refer to this mania, during the last several months, of bringing about scandals or of taking pleasure in thrusting into the limelight real or imaginary scandals.

If wrongdoings take place within the House of Commons, I suggest that there are courts which could settle that. The Canadian people are fed up with the house losing weeks and months wallowing in scandals, when it could get down to the more useful business of passing good legislation for the nation. I suggest that, in the light of this disaffection of public opinion toward the political parties, it is time for the two main parties, and even for the third and fourth, to decide to call a truce for a few months or at least for the time necessary to pass legislation which has been pending for months.
This, Mr. Speaker, brings me to say that I find the Speech from the Throne acceptable, because it embodies a considerable amount of work. These matters have been called "photocopies" and "remnants". I think that perhaps there are so many "remnants" because there has been so much filibuster. Perhaps if there were less filibustering we could pass the legislative program.
There is another reason, Mr. Speaker. It is that there are many new ministers who will need weeks and even months to get to the bottom of their respective departments and therefore to prepare the legislation which the people need. Until they have had the time to do so, therefore, I suggest to my colleagues that we give the government time to approve these remains of legislation which have been pending for months and months.
Mr. Speaker, the riding of Trois-Rivieres which I represent, will develop considerably in the next few years for reasons that I will outline very briefly. Let it be well understood that if I raise this matter, it is because Trois-Rivieres will become a centre of development which will affect the whole province and country because of the bridge which will be built across the St. Lawrence, of the throughway which is under construction and which will connect Chibougamau, Trois-Rivieres and Sherbrooke and extend to the American border, of the super-highway which is being built between Montreal and Quebec city and of the Sidbec complex which will be located right across the river from Trois-Rivieres. In short, for all kinds of similar reasons. We foresee for Trois-Rivieres a tremendous development in years to come.
The city of Trois-Rivieres, one of the oldest French cities in North America-it was founded in 1634-the queen of all newsprint producing cities and also a cultural centre, has certain problems to face.
The Address-Mr. Mongrain
For instance, our grain elevators which come under the jurisdiction of the national harbours board are experiencing difficulties because of some tax changes that were brought in this year. The burden put on grain elevators has become so prohibitive that it is to be feared they may be forced to move elsewhere.
Those grain elevators are most important to the movement of the wheat we sell abroad and if they were exempted from those charges, or compensated in return, I am sure the house would have found the way to solve the problem of the grain elevators of Trois-Rivieres.
I cannot ignore the fact that the city of Trois-Rivieres owes a lot to the previous government as far as its harbour is concerned, because at that time it was represented here by Hon. Leon Balcer who was then minister of transport. The harbour has continued to develop under this government but it will have to be given the opportunity of further development as soon as possible if the city of Trois-Rivieres is to meet the challenge of the tremendous development which will take place in the area within the next two, three, four or five years.
The redistribution of electoral constituencies will also raise a problem. I know that this matter will be discussed at a later date. I hope I am in order if I say a word about it. I was not here when the commission sat. The city of Trois-Rivieres Ouest was removed from the constituency of Trois-Rivieres, even though it is part of a demographic and economic entity to be annexed to Trois-Rivieres in the coming months. It is most inconsistent to remove from the Trois-Rivieres riding the city of Trois-Rivieres Ouest and to join it with Berthier.
Winter navigation, also of concern to our friends from Halifax and the Maritimes, is becoming increasingly important every year in Trois-Rivieres which has become the head of winter navigation.
I should like to reassure my colleagues. After looking at the figures, I doubt it could be said that what comes from Trois-Rivieres would in anyway deprive the Maritime provinces. On the contrary, it contributes to the development of shipping and shortly the Maritimes will benefit, if they do not already do so.
I have several other points to make, Mr. Speaker, but I want to deal immediately with certain problems involving my province, or at least its relations with the rest of Canada.

An hon. member opposite recently suggested that the federal government should establish a department of federal-provincial affairs. I think this is an excellent and timely idea.
But, I say that indeed something should be added. There is always reference to "dominion-provincial relations", but is there not a third level of government called the municipalities, all too often treated with stand-offishness and all too often put off indefinitely.
Municipal government has its own importance, just as federal and provincial governments. Moreover, from the historical viewpoint, it is the most ancient form of government; besides municipal government is, in fact, closest to the people.
Granted, municipalities come under provincial jurisdiction, but I do believe that at the conference table, when the time comes to discuss the distribution of responsibilities among the three levels of government and then the share of fiscal resources that each of those governments should get to meet its responsibilities, the official representatives of the municipalities should be invited to take part in the discussion, so that they no longer be treated as poor relations.
Hon. minister-I mean Mr. Speaker-I am sorry if I make those slips. I shall get used to it in time and I hope you will bear with me and help me with your good advice.
In addition to this last proposal concerning the relations between the federal, provincial and municipal governments which are nearly always strained, and which are dealt with on a piecemeal basis during meetings of ministers and high officials who have other concerns and who, anyhow, cannot follow up those discussions, I would like to suggest that my colleagues study the composition of an agency which was set up in the United States and which has given excellent results. I am speaking of an intergovernmental advisory commission made up of representatives of the three levels of government.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)

Its membership in the United States is made up of three private citizens appointed by the President, three members of the United States Senate, three members of the United States House of Representatives, three officers of the executive branch of the national government, four governors, three state legislators, four mayors and three county officials. Moreover, these 26 members of

the commission are assisted by some 30 staff members made up of specialists in their own field. Of course, it would have to be adapted to conform to our pattern of government, but I think this body could render some outstanding services toward streamlining operations of our governments at the three levels.

Mr. Speaker, I think it is also important to point out one thing. Like many others, I noticed that following the Speech from the Throne, the Prime Minister made a statement to which the newspapers gave this interpretation: The federal government's position toward the provinces is hardening.
If "hardening" means that they will not give the provinces what they are entitled to under the constitution, I am against that. But if "hardening" means that the federal government is beginning to realize that it deserves a better treatment, that the federal government is-to use an expression which is not very parliamentary-getting sick of negotiations by insults and accusations, I think that the government is right to get tougher and stand up straight.
I will now go on quickly to various matters which are more closely related to the welfare of all countries.
I think that some matters, for instance maintaining peace in the world, are of the utmost concern to hon. members. I have nothing to say about that matter because I do not feel qualified and I have full confidence in the competence of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) to solve those problems.
I am satisfied to see that all hon. members want Canada to do whatever it can to maintain peace in the world.
Next year Canada will witness another event which will probably help to reinforce national unity and promote good will among nations, and during which Canada will be in the spotlight. I am referring to the 1967 World Fair. Here again hon. members should restrict their criticism to a minimum and, united, get really behind that extraordinary undertaking which will be for Canada the starting point of a tremendous development.
Mr. Speaker, reference is made also to the constitution. It is said that it should be revised; some even claim that it should be revised at once. I humbly submit my point of view to my colleagues for a more detailed study. I do not think that we shall ever
January 27, 1966

agree on that constitution, that great charter of Canadian life, if we start discussing the matter in this house or on the hustings. I should like again to say this: we should accept and recognize, at the outset, that as members of parliament we still have that sort of election complex which prevents us from seeing things in their true light.
I think we should set up some kind of areopagus, a council of the wisemen of the country, made up of French speaking and English speaking Canadians or of new Canadians who would meditate in silence and then draw up a kind of Canadian Magna Carta, a new constitution. Let them have all the time they need, one, two or three years, even more if necessary; it is only afterwards that it would be wise for us, politicians, to apply ourselves to the study of this Magna Carta and decide on the advisability of adopting it.
At any rate, even though that constitution would eventually have to be revised, I am one of those who believe that, for the time being, we should give an honest and last chance to the present constitution to bear its fruits.
For all Canadians, that will be one way of trying to consolidate what I call Canadianism or patriotism in this country. I would tell my colleagues that at home, in Quebec, we are Canadians in the full sense of the word, we believe in Canadian unity, we are not separatists but we want to be full citizens of Canada. We are not claiming any privileges, we are asking for nothing we have not already contributed.
In my province, the English are members of the family; they have their industries, they go to their churches, they attend their schools; they are members of our clubs and we look upon them as members of the family. When they go before the courts, they are spoken to in their own language and when they deal with the provincial government, they use their own language. That is what we are demanding for all French Canadians throughout the entire country. They want to be full Canadians, not Canadians out of charity.
We are not asking for full bilingualism, Mr. Speaker, because we know that is impossible; it was never our intention to ask people of Toronto or Winnipeg to force themselves to speak French, but we are asking for official bilingualism in all provincial legislatures and in all courts of justice. That is one condition of our being full Canadians.
The Address-Mr. MacRae
We also want the control of all that can deeply affect the way of life of any French Canadian who wants to be a full Canadian. We are loyal to the British crown; we proved it in 1774, 1792, 1812, 1842, 1876, 1914, and 1940 but again if we are to have unity we will have to be considered as full Canadians.
We are tired of being told that we should assimilate. Assimilate to what? Assimilate to whom? We have been assimilated to Canada for 350 years, we have been Canadians for 350 years, we have paid taxes, fought in wars and given the nation great parliamentarians and great businessmen. We no longer want to hear such words as: Remember the Plains of Abraham. I think that words like these only add fuel to the fire and that those who say them are responsible for the deplored separatist movement in Quebec.
For example, I was told during the election campaign that the member for York East (Mr. Otto) and the member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan) apparently said something to the effect that "it is time for French Canadians to assimilate".
I want to tell those colleagues of mine that until I have proof to the contrary, I shall assume that they did not mean to say such things or that they were misquoted by the reporters. If it were true, they should be considered as troublemakers and unworthy of sitting in this house and being members of the Liberal party.
I say again that we, from Quebec, want to be first class Canadians. We want to do our share in this country, but we also want to be put on the same footing as other Canadians.
Once again, Mr. Speaker, I am sorry for my lack of experience and I thank you for your co-operation. Since I do not wish to overtax my colleagues' patience, I shall close my remarks here, so that other members can take part in this debate.
My apologies for this morning's incident, which was not meant to embarrass the house, but rather to try and establish once and for all the principle that the house is willing to respect the prerogatives of each and every member, even if he comes here as a lone wolf.

Mr. Speaker, my first words must be to congratulate you on your elevation to the office you now hold. I have been impressed, as I am sure all hon. members have been over the last few years, by your ability, by your
332	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. MacRae fairness and above all by your sense of humour. I think your ready smile may do much in the months or, it may be, the years ahead to smooth over the rough places in our parliament. If the decision should ever be made that there should be a permanent Speaker I think Your Honour would be given a unanimous vote by this House of Commons.
I should also like to congratulate the Deputy Speaker, who has been a personal friend of mine for many years, and the Deputy Chairman of Committees. My congratulations extend also to the mover (Mr. Goyer) and seconder (Mr. Stanbury) of the address. As the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) said, the maiden speech of any member of the House of Commons is never an easy one. These gentlemen conducted themselves very well indeed.
I could not help but recall, when the hon. member for Dollard (Mr. Goyer) was speaking, a night last June when his predecessor from that constituency sat here while the now famous Dorion report was tabled. I hope the career of the hon. member who now sits for Dollard will come to a happier conclusion than that of his predecessor.
I was interested to hear the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. Stanbury) mention during his remarks that he was speaking for 300,000 constituents. I might point out that if this late, unlamented, and unnecessary election had not been forced upon the people of Canada he might have represented a much smaller number of people when he came here. This is one of the reasons why we should not have had the election which was held last November. I refer to the gross inequities in representation today.
There have been a number of resignations from the government. I think the former minister of finance, the former secretary of state and the former postmaster general followed the only honourable course they could follow in resigning their portfolios. I think there are two others, the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Favreau) and the present Secretary of State (Miss LaMarsh) who might have followed that worthy example. I congratulate those ministers who have been newly appointed to portfolios as well as those who have been promoted, particularly the present Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson), a fellow New Brunswicker who has now held four different portfolios. For the good of this nation I wish him success.
It seems to me that in this nation we face roughly half a dozen basic problems. One of

DEBATES	January 27, 1966
the greatest is the threat of inflation and I should like to discuss this at some length. The second problem I should like to discuss today in the time available to me has reference to what has been called the education explosion.
I see there are a number of items on the order paper relating to another subject which particularly interests me, the importance of fresh water and the polluted state of many of our lakes and rivers. A third question that deeply interests me is the growing number of highway accidents and fatalities. The hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey) has been especially active in this field, one in which a number of members on this side of the house have also taken a keen interest. I think we have reached a point where this House of Commons will have to take action in order to prevent so many people destroying themselves on the highways. Then there is the subject which the previous speaker has raised so eloquently today, the ferment in one of our great founding provinces.
First, I should like to discuss inflation. At this moment there is a question standing on the order paper in my name which asks:
1.	Is the government aware and concerned about
the possibility of inflationary trends in construction prices in this country?	,
2.	If so, what action is the government planning to take about any such trends?
This question was motivated by an item which appeared in the press a few weeks ago reporting that the president of the Canadian Construction Association had warned the nation that there was definitely a grave risk of inflation, that in fact this situation had already come about in the construction industry. It is to such a danger as this that the amendment moved by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) was directed, because it especially concerns the 11 per cent sales tax. I saw another item in the press yesterday under a Canadian Press dateline from Vancouver. This is a terrible thought. It says that in the year 2011 we will be paying $5 a pound for beef. But what is even worse, Mr. Speaker, is that he said we are going to be paying $35 a bottle for Scotch whisky and $750 for a suit. He also goes on to say that the average person's salary, if the present inflationary trend continues and the cost of living continues to increase, will be $23,000 and pensions will be $7,900 a year. Finally, he says:

If the figures seem absurd, go to the newspaper files of 45 years ago and look at what prices were then.

Therefore it seems to me we are definitely faced with a problem of inflation in Canada. The present cost of living is at an all-time high. In September, 1964, according to the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, the consumer price index was 135.6 in relation to a base of 100 in 1949. In 1965, one year later, the consumer price index was 139.1. This is an increase of 3.5 points, or $3J if one wants to look at it that way, or a rise of 2.6 per cent.
Of course what happens with inflation is that it falls most heavily on the small wage earner and on the pensioner who is in receipt of a small pension. I was distressed, as I am sure many hon. members were, by the curt and almost arrogant answer of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) in his reply to a question about federal civil service superannuates. There is a branch of this association in my constituency, and I know one widow who is trying to live as best she can on $39 a month, which is the amount of her deceased husband's pension. I think the point has been well made by many others but I should like to repeat that there should be an escalation clause tied in with the cost of living and attached to the pension schemes of these people, as there should be to all pension schemes.
I have been deeply disturbed by the number of strikes which took place during the past year. It seems to me that in 1965 we had more strikes in this nation-perhaps this is true of the United States, too, because our economies are so closely allied-than we have had for many, many years. Just to digress for a moment, we saw the recent strike in New York city which cost the people of that large metropolis $100 million a day and almost tied it up completely. During the strike this fellow Quill was able, figuratively, to thumb his nose at the mayor of the city and the President of the United States. Sometimes we private members may think we have troubles here but look at the problem of Mayor Lindsay who took office at midnight and five hours later was faced with the New York transportation strike.
Another strike I should like to discuss briefly is that of the vocational students in Quebec which I believe has now come to a conclusion. I read that the premier of Quebec and his minister of education were greatly disturbed by it, and so they should be. Some
25,000	students went out on strike because their school year was extended from June 4 to June 21. High school students and most vocational students-I know whereof I speak
DEBATES	333
The Address-Mr. MacRae because vocational teaching is my profession-attend school until the end of June.
I understand that over the last half dozen years we have spent $1,100,000,000 on the building, equipping and staffing of vocational and technical schools. These students are paid to go to school. It is in their own self-interest that they do so in a world which is changing rapidly, in a world where automation is doing away with jobs that men's hands and in many cases men's minds have been doing for centuries. This is a great opportunity for them to achieve an education, to go out in the labour market and be employed that much sooner; yet they go out on strike. It is a sad commentary on what is happening today. They are paid to go to school. A great many here did not have their opportunity but would have welcomed it.
I should like to discuss the educational explosion and more particularly the report of the Bladen commission. A few figures will highlight what I have to say. In 1953 there were 63,000 students attending university in this nation. In 1960 that figure had risen to 100,000. In 1963 it was 140,000, in 1965, 180,000 and in 1975, according to the Sheffield projection, there will be 461,000 students in universities, more than three times the number of students who were there two years ago.
The cost involved is interesting. It is estimated that in 1965 the cost of university higher education is $355 million. In 1975-76, when there will be approximately twice the number of students who are attending university today, the cost will be $1,704,000,000 or five times the cost today. There will be two and a half times as many students but five times the cost. Therefore I think we must bend all our minds and all our efforts to this problem.
The recommendations of the Bladen commission are worthy of being placed on the record of the house. This commission was set up by the Association of Universities and Colleges of Canada, with the distinguished Dean Bladen as commissioner. Here in part are his recommendations;
1.	That the federal and provincial governments undertake to provide for the expansion of higher education in Canada on the scale of the Sheffield projection.
2.	That the federal government initiate annual discussions with the provincial governments to review the adequacy of the federal contribution to the cost of higher educationthis is rather interesting.
-but that federal support be in a form which avoids any invasion of the provincial right, and obligation, to direct and control such education

January 27, 1966
The Address-Mr. MacRae
3.	That the federal government assign responsibility for co-ordination of assistance to universities from all its agencies to a minister of the crown.
4.	That such minister establish a small advisory committee mainly consisting of senior professors from various regions and disciplines, and appoint a senior civil servant as secretary of that committee and as organizer of the proposed annual discussions with the provinces.
5.	That the financial problems of the universities are so urgent that action to resolve them should be taken without delay.
The commission also made a particular recommendation to the federal government which I am glad to see has already been implemented in part within the last week, namely, that the present per capita grants be raised to $5 for the year 1965-66 and increased by $1 each year thereafter.
There is a further submission I would like to make in connection with the Bladen commission report and it comes from the Association of Atlantic Universities. It is one that is especially important to all of us who come from Atlantic Canada, an area of Canada which, through its universities, has given so many distinguished men and women to this and other nations of the world. The Association of Universities and Colleges of Canada recently presented a submission to the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) based on the findings of the Bladen commission. It asked for more generous equalization payments and urged in the meantime a special grant to maritime universities. Here is the particular point as they made it:
The commission pressed its belief that the special fiscal needs of the less wealthy provinces should be dealt with by general equalization grants.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
That is the principle which the Conservative administration followed between 1957 and 1963 with great benefit, and we in the Atlantic provinces are very grateful for that administration's adherence to this principle.
The association then stated:
We share this conviction. We, therefore, urge the federal government to provide more generous equalization payments to these provinces as quickly as possible. Until such time as increased equalization payments are made, we suggest that a special grant of $3 million per annum be paid to the universities and colleges of the Atlantic provinces in proportion to their number of full time students, who are eligible to be counted in calculating federal per capita operating grants.
Then the association makes a second recommendation which deals with out of province students. There are many out of province students attending universities in the Atlantic provinces, universities such as

St. Francis Xavier and the University of New Brunswick in Fredericton and Dalhousie University in Halifax. Many out of province students come to take forestry and engineering at U.N.B. and in the early days they came to study law at Dalhousie when the late Hon. Sidney Smith was dean of law there. They come to St. Francis Xavier to study the cooperatives.
This measure is of very great importance to our Atlantic provinces' universities because they have such a large percentage of out of province and out of country students. Many Canadian universities have in their enrolments substantial numbers of other provinces' students and students from other countries. We favour the movement of Canadian students from province to province and we welcome the students from other countries.
We are of the opinion that the federal government has a special responsibility to assist universities in financing the cost of educating such students. As a means of discharging this responsibility, we suggest that the federal government should provide a supplementary grant for educating such students according to a formula to be devised in consultation with the provinces and universities. We suggest that the supplementary grants should be made only with the clear understanding that this will not reduce to any extent the grants required to implement the recommendations we have endorsed and recommended. I submit these suggestions for the earnest and sympathetic consideration of the government of this nation.
There was a third point about which the Bladen commission was specific and which will perhaps not be too popular on the hustings if members endorse it. I refer to the recommendation in respect of free tuition. The suggestion of free tuition is an attractive one but we know only too well that nothing is free and that everything we do and everything we buy must be paid for in one way or another. I think it would be unjust and unfair to those Canadians who cannot avail themselves of a university education to have to pay for capital grants and so on through taxes and also pay for others to get an education. For at least some time in the forseeable future I think students should make every effort to pay their own tuition.
It is my belief that there should be scholarships and that their number should be greatly increased. There should, of course, be a student loan plan, but I think a student who has

had loans for perhaps five years will find himself with a heavy burden to carry upon graduation. At that stage of life many of these young men wish to marry and establish homes of their own. In spite of all the difficulties involved I concur in the suggestion of the Bladen commission that those who can afford to pay full tuition fees should pay at least a portion of the cost of a university education.
One other matter which is very close to my heart, and I spoke of this during the last session, concerns between 1,000 and 1,200 men in this country. I refer to the men who were prisoners of war of the Japanese after the fall of Hong Kong in 1941. A number of members in all parties have been urging the minister and the government to give these men some special consideration. The hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Bigg) and the hon. member for Victoria, B.C. (Mr. Groos) are particularly concerned about these Hong Kong veterans.
Those veterans underwent greater hardships than perhaps any of the rest of us who were privileged to serve during world war II. The time they spent in prison camps and the treatment they received are comparable to the suffering of those people who were incarcerated in Hitler's concentration camps. We know something of what happened to those six million people who were dehumanized, brutally treated, starved, tortured and murdered. This is one of the blackest chapters in the history of mankind. There are a number of people in our nation who spent some time in these concentration camps, and I know there are several members of the house who were prisoners of war in Europe. I refer to the hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Mr. Winkler) and the hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. Clancy). There are a number of others who were prisoners of war including the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Teillet).
I was fortunate enough never to have been a prisoner of war but I am sure those who suffered under the hands of the Japanese suffered immeasurably more than others who were relatively fairly treated. I think these men deserve special consideration.
An inquiry was made by Dr. Richardson over the past two years regarding the Hong Kong prisoners of war. The findings of that inquiry are very slow in their final production.
I know it takes time to evaluate matters of this kind and I am happy to see that a slight concession has been made in that these veterans have been given extra dental care. There
