speechtext:
Mr. Deputy Speaker, on rising in the House of Commons for the first time I congratulate you and the Speaker of this house on achieving your present positions. From the many remarks made on both sides of the house it is obvious to those of us who are sitting in this chamber for the first time that the Speaker and yourself are held in the highest regard by all hon. members and that collectively you will carry out your duties with the best interests and integrity of this house as your only objective.
I congratulate the hon. member for Dollard (Mr. Goyer) and the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. Stanbury), the mover and seconder of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. They have set a standard that not only augurs well for the future of this house but is also an example to those of us who are now following them.
The Northwest Territories, the constituency that it is my privilege to represent, is a vast land of many faces, an exciting and frustrating land, the land of the long day where Canadiana, I suggest, has been blended in a way that has not been seen anywhere else in this our nation. Those of us who are fortunate enough to live on Canada's last frontier have a particular pride in our land. We know we face the realities of life, the cold, the wind, the darkness and, for many of our people, hunger and frustration. We know we

DEBATES	January 27, 1966
have around us a heritage of toughness, excitement and hope. We know we have made a contribution to Canada's history, that we are part of Canada's present way of life and, more important, we know we will share in our nation's future. When a northerner comes to southern Canada he sees an affluent society. He becomes concerned about the lack of understanding on the part of our countrymen of our land, our people and our future.
Canada is a northern nation, one which has been blessed by Providence, where the seeds of nature curl up each winter in hibernation to rejuvenate after the winter months in the warm sun of the spring and ripen and blossom into the productivity which makes our country great. By nature's design we are a northern country. We share the roof of the world with Scandinavia, Russia and the United States. Yet are we meeting the challenge of being a northern country? Do we know the extent of our physical resources, the mineral, oil and water potential? Do we know or understand our greatest resource, the people who live there? Collectively as Canadians our answer is less than ideal. Possibly individually, either in a corporate or personal sense, there are some who do understand these things.
However, Mr. Speaker, I am concerned that as a youthful, dynamic, exciting and energetic country we as Canadians are not fully aware of our national identity as a northern country. Sometimes those of us who call the north our home smile benevolently and yet with great concern at the stresses and strains that pull at the foundations of our country. We cannot help but wonder why there is a cleavage, if there is one, between the founding races of confederation. Yet we too are fighting for our identity and we try to understand that Canadian confederation is the grouping together of peoples of various backgrounds and cultures who are anxious to share equally with pride and understanding the fruits of the geographic entity known as Canada.
To many the north is a bewildering and unknown country, the land of snow and ice. To too few Canadians it is the land of opportunity, excitement and the future. We hope that our countrymen will learn more about us and our country as it is in this land that our nation will build its future in the generations to come.
An historic occasion, Mr. Speaker, is taking place on the grounds of parliament hill during the balance of this week and next week
January 27, 1966
with the meeting of the Council of the Northwest Territories. I say "historic" because I am convinced that the Carruthers commission, the commission appointed by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Laing) to determine from the people of the north the form and type of government best suited to that country, will recommend that all future sessions of the Northwest Territories Council be held in the north. This step, combined with the transfer of the Commissioner and his office to the north, will bring territorial government closer to the people of the Northwest Territories.
The hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) made a number of statements last Friday with which, surprisingly enough, I must agree. It is possible that this will be the only time we will see eye to eye on any subject. He advocated the transfer of many of the powers now held by the federal government to the territorial governments of both the Yukon and Northwest Territories. He specifically referred to the transfer of such matters as land administration. He pointed out the difficulties of dealing with an administration centred thousands of miles from the scene of activity.
The logic of this argument makes much sense and should be the basis of planning now. I hope that when the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources sponsors amendments to the Northwest Territories Act he will provide this house with a meaningful blueprint which will detail greater autonomy for the territorial government combined with a timetable for the transfer of functions that are territorial in nature to the territorial government.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
I am hopeful, too, that the bill can be dealt with expeditiously in order that the franchise may be extended to those citizens of the eastern Arctic who are now unable to vote in territorial elections. There have been suggestions that possibly the principle of appointing members to the Council of the Northwest Territories be abolished. The majority of elected members past and present have consistently acknowledged the contribution of the appointed members. These men serve without pay and sometimes at great inconvenience to themselves. The councillors are strongly in favour of retaining appointed members of council at least for the foreseeable future. This fact too will be examined by the Carruthers commission, and I believe it
The Address-Mr. Orange is only proper to await the commission's recommendations before expressing our personal opinions on this subject.
One of the disturbing factors that has been suggested on a number of occasions in the past few years has been the somewhat rude and intolerable suggestion on the part of provincial representatives of two of the western provinces that the boundaries of these provinces be extended north to absorb the Yukon Territory and Northwest Territories into those provinces. Let me make it clear that northerners have no desire to become part of any nefarious scheme of this nature. We find it somewhat strange and disconcerting that this interest has been generated only after the oil and mineral potential of the Yukon, Mackenzie and Arctic have become a reality.
For many years, the Northwest Territories were virtually ignored by our provincial cousins in the same way that many parts of the northern areas of the provinces were ignored by their governments. Now that the resources of the north are becoming a major factor in spurring the development of our country, it becomes obvious to us why there are those who are casting covetous eyes on our territories. To know northern people is to understand them and to understand them is to appreciate them and the pride they have in themselves and in their land. We want to develop our own institutions and political entities. We are not interested in being swallowed up in a Louisiana type land grab by any of the provinces.
Northerners are strong for political autonomy, the opportunity to run their own affairs and to participate in the development of their own country. They recognize that they have neither the population nor the resources to do it on their own. They acknowledge the impetus given to this progress by the government of Canada, particularly during the last decade, and are anxious to see it continued and, more important, increased. The end results will be to build a strong north fitting within the framework of Canadian confederation and contributing to Canadian society. It is freely acknowledged by people who know northern Canada and its economic potential that the future of the country rests with the mining industry. If we are to grow and prosper we must see new mines come into production and our people trained to participate in this development.

338	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Orange
There are two serious problems facing all or part of the mining industry today. There exists throughout Canada a severe labour shortage in the mining industry. In the July, 1965, edition of the publication, Today in Mining, the official journal of the Mining Association of Canada, the managing director of the association is quoted as saying that there are more than 4,000 men needed this year across Canada to fill a wide range of technical, skilled and unskilled jobs. This figure could be higher, the general manager goes on to say, since some companies were not in a position to forecast their requirements at that time. I have been told by the managers of mines that some of the mines in our more isolated or marginal areas could be forced into a position of cutting back on their operations and, in one particular instance, possibly closing unless there is improvement in the labour supply. I am hopeful that perhaps a new training program for unskilled and partly trained workers will take into account the urgent needs of the mining industry, an industry which in Canada affords employment directly or indirectly to approximately 13 per cent of our national labour force and accounts for 7.2 per cent of our gross national product.
A second and equally important point of concern is the possibility that the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act will be allowed to expire in 1967. This act was extended in 1963 for four additional years. I can think of no way of retarding northern development more than by not extending this act beyond 1967. It is equally important that the decision in this regard be made as early as possible in order that the industry may be assured of further government assistance to give it an opportunity to schedule its work beyond the present expiry date of the act. If this measure is not extended, I can foresee the closing of mines in the Northwest Territories which would be a serious blow to the development of the north.
At the same time, there is a provision in the act which I believe should be re-examined. It is my understanding that assistance under the act does not apply to any new mine which came into operation after June 30, 1965, unless this mine is located in an area which is presently classified as a gold mining community and where the majority of the persons employed in the mine would normally live in the community. In other words, the way the act is framed at the

DEBATES	January 27, 19G6
present time it is virtually impossible for a northern gold mine to be brought into production or operation unless it is located in the immediate vicinity of the thriving nortropolis of Yellowknife.
During the next few weeks the house will have an opportunity to discuss the organization of the new department of Indian affairs and northern affairs. I hope to have an opportunity of expressing my views at that time on the role and place of our first Canadians in present day society. It has occurred to me, however, that the proposed name of the department might be changed. I should like to think that a possible name for the department might be the department of Indian, Eskimo and northern affairs to give recognition to the contribution our Eskimo people have made to Canadian society.
Like many of our colleagues, I am concerned and worried about the rate of progress being made in bringing some Indian and Eskimo people into the mainstream of Canadian life and giving them the same opportunity for education and human development that other Canadians now have as a birthright. It is not easy to go into an Indian community and to accept the squalor, deprivation and despair you may find in many communities, where even basic amenities such as power, water and decent housing are unknown.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
I suggest that there is not an Indian problem in Canada but there is a white problem, a problem of the lack of understanding of the Indian people and their culture. A philosophy has been developing over the years that the Indian people are wards of the government. Fortunately, this thinking is changing, but we must ask ourselves whether it is changing fast enough and must we wait for generations to see the results.
In the northern parts of the provinces and in the Yukon and Northwest Territories many Indian and Eskimo people continue to hunt and trap as their forefathers have done before them. This way of life is a hard and for the most part an unrewarding means of existing. Since world war II the price of furs and skins has been steadily declining while costs to the producer, the man living in the bush or on the tundra, have increased at a rate comparable with the rest of Canada. The result has been a great increase in welfare payments to our native peoples combined with a general decline in the trapping industry. The obvious effects of welfare in place of
January 27, 1968	COMMONS
work require no amplification. I would recommend to the government that serious consideration be given to the establishment of a floor price on furs and skins which would bring stability to a wildly fluctuating industry, and at the same time provide a means whereby a man who wishes to pursue this means of livelihood will feel that he can support his family and himself in dignity.
It may be argued that fur is a luxury item and should not receive any form of government support. Granted it is a luxury item to the fashion model in Montreal or Toronto, but to the hunter and trapper it is a means of support. I believe strongly that should stability be brought to the fur industry welfare payments would decrease in direct proportion to the subsidy or floor price. Even more important, many of our Indian and Eskimo peoples would become productive citizens of our society, gaining in the self-respect that comes from economic independence.
I suggest also that the concept of a floor price or subsidy is not unknown in our Canadian society. If we are to attract settlers into the north of Canada, I think we must do so in a way that acknowledges that there are differences in the cost of living between northern Canada and the south, that many of the amenities enjoyed by our countrymen in the south are not readily available in northern Canada.
At this time I should like to make note of the contribution the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has made to our northern way of life. The northern service of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, either through local radio stations or by means of shortwave, covers much of northern Canada. The corporation is to be congratulated on the initial steps it has taken in extending radio services throughout the north. I would like to think that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation's progress to date has reached a plateau from which they intend to launch further advancements.
One of the problems facing northern residents is the lack of recreation. Because of the extreme weather conditions outdoor recreation is virtually impossible for most of the winter. At the same time we have read press reports that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is intending to develop a colour television network in southern Canada in the near future. Yet I understand there are no firm plans to bring television services to those areas of Canada which do not enjoy this benefit. I would hope that there would be a
DEBATES	339
The Address-Mr. Fulton rethinking of the C.B.C.'s plans in order to bring a combination of live television to those areas where it is economically feasible, such as the southern Mackenzie, or to establish semi-automated videotape stations where live television is impractical. I would like to see this happen before a colour television network is developed for the populated areas of southern Canada.
The headquarters of the northern service of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation are located in Montreal. Programming is controlled from this centre. In the Mackenzie district there is a hook-up with the prairie service of the C.B.C. With the exception of national news reports newscasts in the north are not of topical interest to the listeners to the Mackenzie network. It seems to me that if the C.B.C. were to pursue their radio network to its logical conclusion, the headquarters of the northern service would be located in the north together with such features as a northern newsroom.
In concluding my remarks, Mr. Speaker, may I express the fervent prayer that the members of this house will deal with the nation's business in a way that will give to the people of Canada confidence and pride in the activities of their representatives in parliament.

Mr. Speaker, at this stage of the debate, I wish to say a few words to congratulate you sincerely on your appointment as Speaker of the house. The qualities you have already shown, prove that our choice was a wise one. We are pleased to have such a competent and distinguished man to chair our proceedings.

I should like to add too my felicitations to those who have been chosen to serve with you in the office of Deputy Speaker and the other offices of the house, and to wish them and you every happiness in the discharge of your responsibilities with the assurance of our support in that task.
I am in a position, Mr. Speaker, where I crave the indulgence of the house to make a personal reference for a brief moment or two. I am returning to the house after an absence. I am not sure whether I am making a maiden speech or not but I hope I will be given the indulgence that maiden speeches are usually accorded in this place. I should like to express my very grateful thanks for the
340	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Fulton warmth of the welcome I have been given by my colleagues both inside and outside the chamber.
I appreciate that welcome the more in that I am following, as the member for the federal constituency of Kamloops, Dr. Charles Willoughby, a member of parliament who, together with his wife, in the comparatively short space of time that they were here endeared themselves to everyone as well as establishing a remarkable record for faithful and effective service to their constituency. I hope that the career I follow here in the future will be worthy of the example that he set.
I have referred to my absence for a short period. This absence gave me time for reflection. It contained one or two incidents which I hope will not be repeated, such as a defeat in an election, but it did serve as a profitable opportunity for reflection. It also had the effect, that as absence gives time for reflection, so the return makes me perhaps the more happy. Because I have returned to the greatest of Canadian institutions, the House of Commons in the parliament of Canada, and who could help but be happy at being back in that institution.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
I have tried during that absence to keep in touch with issues in general, with the discussions in parliament and with the changes in the rules which have taken place and which are now being tried out. I realize I have much to learn on my return but I hope I shall be able, along with my colleagues, to serve effectively this great institution of which we are members.
I have appreciated the difficult period through which my hon. friends in the House of Commons have been passing during the last three years. If one were to believe everything one reads in the press-and I have learned not to accept it all as gospel-one would think that parliament was in imminent danger of collapse. There have been difficulties, it is true, and I appreciate those difficulties fully, but it seems to me we can preserve a sense of proportion about those difficulties by realizing that the country itself is going through a difficult period.
Canada is today facing a situation as crucial as any it has faced in the past as it comes to the point of determining the direction- national, economic, political and cultural-that it will take. It seems to me that the difficulties experienced in parliament were but a reflection of the state of the nation. As yet no

DEBATES	January 27, 19G6
clear cut decisions have been taken with respect to these questions. The country has not decided and it should therefore be not surprising that parliament has been undecided and at times divided and that this chamber should now be a house of minorities.
This is the decision the people made last November 8. The government, it appears to me, cannot avoid a large share of the responsibilty for the indecision and lack of direction I have mentioned since it is the responsibility of the government to give leadership and direction. I will say more along these lines at other stages of the session. But the main thing, to my mind, is that we should accept our responsibility here, the responsibility of all of us, difficult though the circumstances may be, to make this institution work.
May I say a further word on the subject because there seems a danger when discussing this matter of co-operation and making the institution work, ends to which each one of us is dedicated, that one might be taken as meaning there should not be division on important issues. We must have divisions on issues and the opposition must constructively oppose where real issues are involved. I am certain many such issues will arise this session. The Speech from the Throne, if fulfilled, contains many issues on which there must be debate and division of opinion on a philosophical basis, issues such as the one we shall be voting on tonight, matters on which a marked and legitimate difference of opinion may be expected. Surely co-operation such as has been asked for and extended does not and cannot mean there should not be vigorous and proper opposition. That is the duty of opposition in this house. I assure you, sir, and all members of this house it is in this spirit I shall attempt to make my contributions to the discussions in which we shall be taking part.
It is in this spirit I should like to turn to consideration of the Speech from the Throne. It is, I believe, a legitimate criticism to say that this speech lacks the sense of direction for which parliament and the country are crying out. I recognize the presence in the Speech from the Throne of forecasts of legislation and programs to deal with real issues. But it does not appear to me to be an adequate document to set the pattern for making Canada great. The problems which confront Canada today are not just those which can be solved by spending money on welfare, desirable though it may be to do this. It seems to me the real problems of
January 27, 1966	COMMONS
Canada today can only be solved by challenging our people to take thought for the future and by giving them the sense of direction for which they are waiting so anxiously. There is no single thought of this responsibility of government which emerges from the Speech from the Throne.
I should like to mention one specific area of challenge, one of great difficulty for the future of Canada, an area in which we are entitled to expect the government and this parliament to challenge the resourcefulness of our people as we are now challenging the government, inviting them to indicate whether sacrifices of short term interest should not be made in order that we may profit by sound plans for the long term future. I am referring particularly here to the area of a national water resources policy, surely one of the most pressing questions with which we are now faced, one which is truly urgent in terms both of its size and of its opportunities, urgent also in view of the shortness of time available for its disposal if we are not to find ourselves in a grave situation. It is most disturbing to find no reference to a national water resources policy in the Speech from the Throne in 1966.
We believe that criticism by the opposition should be matched by constructive proposals and I will therefore suggest for the consideration of the government and of the house some elements which I feel should be incorporated in and be the objects of any national water resources policy.
I would place first the following objective: To preserve and ensure the availability of an adequate supply of pure, clean water for Canada's present and future needs. Having said this, hardly anything more is needed to demonstrate the size and the urgency of the problem with which we are faced. Second, our object should be to ensure the best distribution of water within Canada. We do have areas which are rich in water and others which are water-poor. We must ensure, for instance, that the prairies are served with adequate supplies of water. We must ensure also that there is a fair distribution within areas. For example, in certain areas, such as the one from which I come, there is land which would profit enormously from irrigation while there is water not too far distant which could be used for this purpose.
Third, having accomplished our first two objectives we should seek to ensure the optimum use within Canada of these resources.
DEBATES	341
The Address-Mr. Fulton Here we should perhaps pause for a moment to reflect upon the many vital uses of water and of the potential conflict between these uses so as to illustrate the size of what is involved. Consider the ways in which water is used, for domestic consumption, for sewage and other municipal purposes, for fishing, boating and similar recreational purposes, for transportation along the great waterways and canal systems, for industrial uses and for many other purposes essential to the vital needs of a modern society.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
We must therefore tackle now the problem of reconciling the potential conflict between these uses and assure that no one use is allowed to interfere unduly with the other uses I have mentioned and which are equally essential. This can only be done if criteria are established on a national basis for the maintenance of an adequate supply of pure water.
Such criteria, it seems to me, will differ of course from river basin to river basin and from location to location even within a basin, but we must take thought now to plan for the reconciliation of these multiple uses. After all, those responsible for city planning and the location of industry must have such criteria if they are to be able to plan precisely.
Fourth, I would mention as among the aims of national policy in this sphere the establishment and maintenance of a Canadian position, a Canadian policy, before ever entering upon any discussions with regard to the diversion or alienation of any Canadian waters.

But only an adequate national policy, a preconceived and sound Canadian policy in connection with water can be allowed to form the basis of a rational response to these overtures from the United States. In other words, the Canadian position, protecting Canadian interests present and future, must be established before any negotiation is commenced on water diversion, and it must be maintained during that negotiation.
Fifth and finally, I would suggest that among the aims of national policy must be to ensure that when and if negotiations are
January 27, 1966

The Address-Mr. Fulton commenced adequate recompense for this Canadian resource, or such part of it as we
may then decide on the basis of policy is available for joint use, must be secured to Canada for that priceless asset.
I have spoken of the urgency of the problem in terms of its size and of the time factor and I would like to demonstrate this urgency and the practical importance of working out this policy by reference to two or three examples. I think of the situation in my own constituency, or such part of it as will be left when the redistribution commission is through with it. I think of a part in the very centre of my constituency at the junction of the North and South Thompson rivers, rivers which again are typical of the beauties and the diversity of the present Canadian water supply, and also of the problems that are to be faced if we are to preserve this supply in its splendor-fishing and recreational rivers, rivers which are used for irrigation, for domestic consumption and, in growing measure, for industry.
This area now has a growing problem, a pressing problem with respect to the setting up of a water users community, again so as to reconcile these interests, to ensure that multiple use can be made of the supply instead of one use overriding another. There is a pressing problem in this respect. Also we have Indian reserves on both those rivers, and up and down their banks, and they are also concerned and affected. It is a problem in which it is quite obvious that an effective solution is going to require the assistance of the senior levels of government both provincial and federal. It is a problem which cannot be much longer deferred.
Naturally, as one does, I think of the situation in my riding, but I think also of situations elsewhere in Canada, of the situation on the great lakes with respect to navigation and pollution, particularly lake Erie, described by spokesmen who are not alarmists in this field as already being a dead lake. I think of the situation below these parliament buildings in the Ottawa river, a river which has been described, again by informed spokesmen in this field, as being more polluted than the Rhine, that great artery of commerce in Europe which has been used for thousands of years. How long have we been using the Ottawa? Just for a flash of time in history, but already the Ottawa river is more polluted than the Rhine in Europe.
Other members, I know, have similar problems in their areas, and it will be a national


crime if we let this problem go on any longer without taking thought to clear up the mess of pollution where it exists and to prevent further pollution of our supplies of water. After all, if we allow a situation to become a crisis it is always vastly more expensive to cure it than if you take thought for the future and plan to prevent the crisis from arising.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I would again like to suggest for the consideration of the government and the house what might be some first steps in the process of devising such a national water resources policy. Of course, it is first of all necessary to recognize that this is a field of divided jurisdiction. This being the case, waters within provincial boundaries being provincial resources and yet there being so many areas of federal jurisdiction involved in their use and control, it follows as a matter of course that the most complete consultation must be commenced with the provinces at the earliest possible date in order to work out an agreed water resources policy.
I would like to refer to the statement of principle made on behalf of this party by its leader in March, 1964, when he said:
Conservation of water is a necessity for Canadian growth .... A dominion-provincial survey should be made of our waters to the end that, in co-operation with the provinces, we will assure that water resources shall be available for future generations.
He went on to stress that national action was needed to meet the problem. Toward the end of my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I want to return to the question of national action and national responsibility, and of co-operation between the national and the provincial governments.
At the same time as we must institute discussions leading to a co-operative policy on water resources, it is necessary to have co-ordination of the multiplicity of federal agencies now operating in this field. In this connection one can think of some of the departments such as the Department of Public Works with respect to navigable rivers, the Department of Transport with respect to control of navigation on waterways, the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, the International Joint Commission-all these different areas of jurisdiction and all in many cases acting without any co-ordination of policy.
This is hardly to be wondered at, for they are no more than following the lead of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and of the

Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Laing) who speak with two completely different voices on this important matter of whether we should sell our water to the United States. I have already mentioned as one of the heads of urgency in this regard the need for a national or Canadian policy on water resources if the federal government is to respond in Canada's best interests to the mounting pressure from the United States for diversion of Canadian water. It seems to me that we cannot take a dog in the manger attitude. I am as concerned as the Minister of Northern Affairs about the preservation of Canadian interests but I do not think it is possible that we can just sit here and say: No, we won't even discuss it with you, and maintain that position forever. We have to look at the realities of the situation.
The shortage of pure water is now acute in the United States. We remember the fact that last summer the New York authorities had to
DEBATES	343
The Address-Mr. Fulton impose a fine of $50 if a waiter served a glass of water in a restaurant unless a customer specifically requested it. The President has informed Congress that every major river system in the United States is now polluted. Incidentally, this should be an example for Canada to proceed while there is still time to prevent that situation from arising in Canada.
I think one can say with perfect fairness that one of the reasons that pressure for diversion arises in the United States is that they have been profligate in their use of water resources. They used to say: We will never have a problem, we have all the water that we could ever contemplate needing. Now they face a crisis situation, so that we now observe the great and mounting interest shown by the United States concerning the diversion of Canadian water, and the future will certainly bring more pressing requests for more diversion.
In 1963 the public works committee of the United States Senate reported that by the year 2000 the United States will need one thousand billion gallons of water every day but that even under the most ideal conditions only 650 billion gallons a day will be available from domestic sources. We must profit by their mistakes and make sure that this does not happen in Canada.
Second, in order to prepare for Canada's own future water needs and to respond in Canada's best interests to United States demands, the federal government must begin to act now in working out a new Canadian water resources policy on which, and on which alone, we would then be prepared to enter into any discussions with regard to this problem.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I want to mention briefly the constitutional question that is involved. I have spoken of the need for consultation with the provinces, for we must recognize the divided jurisdiction in respect of water resources. Such consultation, planning and programming must not be in a competitive spirit but in a truly co-operative spirit. This can happen and we have seen it happen before provided there is complete consultation at every stage and that the consultation is initiated before any fixed positions are enunciated which will affect anything within the jurisdiction of the other parties. In this regard I think of the happy history of the federal-provincial co-operation in the negotiation of the St. Lawrence Seaway and the Columbia River Treaty in so far as the use of the waters themselves were concerned.

The Address-Mr. Fulton
It has surprised me, and I am sure this concerns members of this house as it concerns the provinces, that this present government which talks about co-operative federalism has produced a Speech from the Throne that positively bristles with intrusions into the sphere of provincial jurisdiction. It bristles with these intrusions. No wonder the provinces are angry and express growing concern when you see this trend multiplied in the Speech from the Throne.
In this whole field of resources development there is room for real co-operation; yet this is practically ignored in the Throne Speech. Here there is room for co-operation of a type which would not be an intrusion into someone else's jurisdiction and here is an area of really urgent problems. I think it is to be greatly regretted, and I am using mild words deliberately, that a government, faced with these problems and with these great opportunities of establishing bases of co-operation, should neglect them in favour of almost exclusive intrusions into fields of social security which are primarily the responsibility of the provinces. Important as these fields may be, we are entitled to complain about the neglect of these other fields.
There is also, of course, in this field great need and justification for the taking of federal initiative, first because this area already lies partly in federal jurisdiction and, second, because this is an area in which there can be effective Canadian action only if there is national co-ordination and policy creation.
Let us consider the question of pollution alone. Some say this is a matter that should be left to the localities or provinces. Localities and provinces cannot take adequate action in this field. We all know of the great competition there is in attracting industry to various locations. How, for instance, can one city enact effective anti-pollution measures only to see attractive industries going to other provinces where there are no such measures? In addition, how can the poorer provinces enact effective anti-pollution measures and at the same time attract industry unless all of Canada, including every province, has anti-pollution measures in effect?
This is not only a problem for federal action and initiative with need and justification in areas such as this; this water use, control and conservation problem is common to all Canadians. This is a Canadian resource from which Canadians benefit, wherever they live, and to the preservation of which they are equally entitled.


Here then is where we can, by agreeing on our objectives, take some beneficial action. I am sure if we agree on the objectives first it will be much easier to agree on the jurisdiction and levels of responsibility which should be assumed by the respective governments. If you start talking about jurisdiction first, somebody immediately becomes suspicious that we are trying to muscle them out. Here is an area where, by agreeing on the objectives in respect of a Canadian water resources policy, we can make real progress in moving toward constitutional harmony in Canada.

With your leave, Mr. Speaker, I shall now deal with a matter which is always close to my heart, Canadian broadcasting and television to which I have devoted 16 years of my life. I am thinking particularly of CKBL and CKBL-TV, of Matane, CJLR, of Quebec City, CKBM, of Montmagny and CHGB, of La Pocatiere, to mention only a few.

Here I have a special thought for the ex-member for Port Arthur, whom I used to tease on this subject every once in a while. I take this opportunity to wish him well in his new activities.

I have carefully read and reread what we generally refer to as the Fowler report. The reading and study of such a voluminous document have left me somewhat perplexed. However, I agree with the committee's views when it says:
It is for parliament to define the goals of the public enterprise and to ensure that the goals assigned to a public agency are achieved. It must say clearly what it wants the broadcasters to do. In the past, Parliament has not stated the goals and purposes for the Canadian broadcasting system with sufficient clarity and precision, and this has been more responsible than anything else for the confusion in the system and the continuing dissatisfaction which has led to an endless series of investigations of it.
Therefore, this leads me, naturally, to ask the government to appoint as soon as possible a committee of the house on radio and television broadcasting in Canada. Such a committee would then enable the elected representatives of the people to choose from the various political parties, to study carefully this touchy question which ceaselessly has regular repercussions in the house, and to find the best solution. It would surely be preferable to setting up, as suggested, a Canadian Broadcasting Board whose chairman would have almost dictatorial powers. Private enterprise is right, in my humble opinion, in dreading and rejecting it completely, as the C.B.C. has already done through its chairman, Mr. Alphonse Ouimet.
January 27, 1966

The Address-Mr. Berger
On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, to allay such apprehensions as may be felt on hearing this, I wish to specify that, for most obvious reasons, parliament should not become the sole director of Canadian radio and television, for then the remedy would be worse than the present ill. What is needed, I feel, is retention of the present system of the Board of Broadcast Governors and the C.B.C., plus a more detailed and clearer definition of their duties, responsibilities and prerogatives.
It is obvious that there is a good deal of unrest in the C.B.C., and the numerous complaints heard in this House or elsewhere are surely warranted. The C.B.C. is admittedly competent in radio and television, as shown by its 1964-65 annual report which mentions the awards and trophies won by the C.B.C.
In 1963, the C.B.C. was awarded 61 prizes and trophies in various national and international events. As regards the educational field, the C.B.C. was awarded six prizes by Ohio University in its 28th contest. Twice in three years, the C.B.C. was awarded a prize by the Spanish Broadcasting Corporation for its French "tele-theatre" in 1963. I suggest that the hon. members should examine that report so as to be fully informed in this regard. At the same time, there are too many radio and television programs that are of a questionable character, arrogant, in poor taste and sometimes pernicious.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
Therefore, a democratic means should be found to censure, if need be, the C.B.C. if the corporation cannot practise self-discipline. So complex is its administration that it is impossible to know exactly who is to blame or who deserves praise, as the case may be.
This led a parliamentary correspondent to say or, rather, write recently:
When Mr. J. Alphonse Ouimet was asked if he did not think it was about time to find out who was running things at the C.B.C., he replied: "We always know, but no names may be mentioned."
The usual dodge. Well, Mr. Speaker, it is time to put a stop to that. Such an arrogant and offhanded way of dealing with things and people can no longer be tolerated.
Considering the ever increasing budgets, am I not right in suggesting that the government must each year make up the deficit of this crown corporation?
I think it would be quite normal to have a standing committee of the house to fully examine every year the financial and other operations of the C.B.C., find solutions to the problems facing the corporation and, of

course, make suggestions, if necessary, toward improving the corporation's services and programs. We would thus save the time expended on asking questions of the responsible minister who then passes them on to the corporation and finally comes up with evasive answers that are not in the least informative, and this is extremely unpleasant for everybody.
On the other hand, private companies- incidentally, they were treated rather harshly in the Fowler report-would have everything to gain in airing their grievances before the said parliamentary committee. Both sides would gather valuable data, learn about new developments and most probably also have the opportunity to see matters in a different light, which would not be a bad thing.
It is most unfortunate that the royal commission could not acknowledge the great services rendered to their respective communities by private stations for the benefit of various associations, welfare organizations and others.
With regard to the many services which can be rendered by private enterprise, I was deeply shocked to learn recently, in my own riding, that some federal civil servants were advised to curry favour with the management of private radio stations in order to be allowed free broadcasting of announcements, because their department did not have money available for this.
If we consider the financial problems inevitably facing the small broadcasting companies in some areas, this way of doing things is unthinkable.
The Canadian Broadcasters Association, a body representing 228 private radio stations and 55 private television stations, including the C.T.V. network, has just submitted to the Secretary of State (Miss LaMarsh) its reply to the notorious Fowler report.
The association dismissed outright the proposal for the setting up of a broadcasting control board. It is not the only one to do so. I received a letter today from a radio station in my riding which reads in part as follows:
(a)	We are opposed to the establishment of a broadcasting control board, because it would entrust to one man only the authority to decide what the Canadian stations must offer their listeners.
We are in favour of an impartial control similar to that of the present Board of Broadcast Governors.
(b)	We wish government authorities would take into account the financial means of local stations when working out their policy on broadcasting inasmuch as the income of the stations is not as large as that available in larger centres. It is not
January 27, 1966

possible for us to offer programs as elaborate as those produced by stations in large cities or by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation's stations.
(c)	In view of the limited staff of local stations such as ours, it would be desirable that the reports required be reduced to a bare minimum, as they involve a large amount of work.
Those were a few notes I received today from Station CKBL in Montmagny.
Well, Mr. Speaker, the association, on the contrary, advocates the maintenance of the present Board of Broadcast Governors, but with this qualification that the number of members should be reduced to three. The latter would, however, work on a full-time or permanent basis. The suggestion deserves consideration, although it does not appeal to me, because of a certain natural distrust of agencies that have a very limited staif, and are thus more subject to undue pressures.
On the other hand, the Association is of the opinion that the C.B.C. should not be forced to extend its services to remote areas. They claim, for instance, that no reason warrants the extension of the corporation's services to the Yukon before the corporation has set up stations in areas already served by private stations.
Broadcasters think that it should be established that in every part of the country there should be room for a private and a public television station.
This somewhat ambiguous quotation makes me think of the difficulty involved in bringing television to an area which I know quite well, that part of the large riding of my desk partner here in the house which we call "the Lower North Shore", in the county of Saguenay. In my opinion it is imperative that, contrary to what is advocated by the Association, the C.B.C. backs up financially the private station which serves this region and which has had to make numerous sacrifices of all sorts in order to satisfy as adequately as possible the legitimate claims of the population of a region topographically so rough and uneven.
Another interesting point in the private stations' reply deserves attention, even if this brings down upon me the ire of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Benson). It is the following:
The association finally is trying to destroy the myth that private stations are making money hand over fist. They complain that Canada and the United States are the only countries where radio and television stations have to pay taxes. In other countries, they imply, radio and television stations are considered as essential public services, consequently tax-exempt, whereas, in addition to these taxes, Canadian stations have to pay the cost of a permit.
I sincerely believe there is food for thought in this, and at the risk of repeating myself, I
The Address-Mr. Berger feel a committee of the house could more carefully study this question.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I will endorse some of the Fowler report findings, flavoured somewhat with my own humble contributions.

But first, will you allow me to quote certain paragraphs of an article published on this matter by the Edmonton Journal, which read as follows:
Why not recognize the C.B.C. internally (as Mr. Fowler recommends with chapter and verse); have parliament define its objectives (as Mr. Fowler also recommends); give it a realistic annual grant; forget about competing with private broadcasters for sponsors; and then give Canadians the best broadcasting service that can be devised?
Then examine the product, year by year, in parliamentary committee and comprehensively at the end of five years. That should show whether T.V, indeed has a potential beyond simple home entertainment and, equally important, whether Canadians want an egghead-program network. After having seen it, five years should be enough to find out.
By then, too, no longer having a subsidized C.B.C. as a commercial competitor, private networks would have a fair chance to demonstrate the best in private broadcasting.
This general approach, it seems to us, would hold far more promise of achievement than putting C.B.C. and private broadcasters under one Canadian broadcasting authority, dictating their programming and then telling them to fight it out for ratings and sponsors.
This too, I believe, Mr. Speaker, is worth a second thought.

Coming back to the Fowler report we find on page 269:
It will be seen that our concept of the future needs for private and public radio in Canada are different. The lines of development of the two have tended to diverge. Private radio has become more and more local and has seriously neglected its national and international responsibilities. CBC radio has concentrated on its national function and has not sufficiently met local needs and the needs of particular segments of the audience. We believe that the trends of both private and public radio should alter and their lines of development should converge, although they can never meet completely.
Private radio stations, while maintaining their flexible and generally valuable local services, should participate more extensively in the national purposes of Canadian broadcasting. Their facilities should be used to interpret different regions of Canada to each other.
That is a most appropriate remark.
Their considerable assets-both financial and cultural-should be mobilized to produce more balanced, more varied, and better program fare for the listeners of each station. Programs that would be beyond the reach and the means of a single station can be produced by merging their
348	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Rynard
assets and their talents. This should be done preferably by voluntary co-operation between the private stations. The basis of this proposition is quite simple. As we conceive it, the performance of a private station must be a valid part of the Canadian broadcasting system. It is not good enough if one station concentrates on news and public information, another on classical music, another on rock-and-roll.
Each station, perhaps with differing emphasis, must expose its listeners to the complete spectrum of radio services. If it cannot do this from its own resources, means must be found to mobilize the resources of several stations to achieve the desired result by co-operative action.
The C.B.C. should revise as soon as possible its administrative framework in order to stop the unfortunate infiltration within its own staff-noted in the last few years-of separatists, subversive elements or others, and there are others, believe me, whom I shall not name but whom I could easily pinpoint and who have probably been the cause of some sharp but well deserved criticism of the Corporation.
The report read on:
For C.B.C. radio the future course of development we suggest is different. It now does reasonably well in providing a national service, but it is rigid, remote, out of touch with local reality.
It must get down into the market-place, not only in its commercial policy. It must establish better contact with local and regional opinion. It too must become a complete service.
For both public and private broadcasting, radio is the great chance. It is the real communicator, the vital interpreter. Television is muscle-bound by its high costs and the consequent need to reach mass audiences.
As was so wisely mentioned by the hon. member for the Northwest Territories (Mr. Orange) who spoke before me.
The report further states:
Radio is mobile and flexible.
It is up to us to make use of it.
To all radio broadcasters we say: Free your radio policies from the shackles of past practices and traditions. Get going.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I hope all hon. members of this house will gladly and quickly make theirs that motto "Get going", in the best interest of the Canadian people, by getting down to work quietly and efficiently in Parliament.

Mr. Speaker, may I congratulate you on your appointment as Speaker and would you also convey to the Deputy Speaker my very best wishes. I realize, as do all of us, that it takes the wisdom of a Solomon and a man of iron
DEBATES	January 27, 1966
will to control the house from the Chair and to keep perfect order. I am sure that those qualities are possessed in no small measure by the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker.
I should also like to convey my congratulations to the mover (Mr. Goyer) and the seconder (Mr. Stanbury) of the Speech from the Throne. I think they did an excellent job. Their topics were dealt with well and they did their task with minimum reference to notes, which speaks well for them in the house. On listening to the newcomers in this house I have been impressed by the excellent quality of their speeches. First of all, Mr. Speaker, may I say I was a little disappointed in the Throne Speech. There were very few priorities as such. Second, I should like to refer to the Department of Transport and deal with a matter particularly concerning my own riding and also the whole of Canada. I refer to an order issued by the Department of Transport which required certain repairs and additions to be made to two of the boats that sail on the great lakes, the Keewatin and the Assinihoia.
Both of those boats were built on the Clyde. In 1907 they were brought across the ocean under their own steam and at the Welland canal were divided into two, being put together again in the Buffalo shipyards. They then sailed up to the great lakes to go into service for the C.P.R. First of all they sailed from Owen Sound to Fort William and Port Arthur and later from Port McNicoll which is at the lower end of Georgian Bay 85 miles north of Toronto and became their home port. It is just a short drive from Toronto by highway 400. From here they have sailed over the years to Fort William and Port Arthur carrying passengers and freight.
Now, Mr. Speaker, 60 per cent or better of the passengers are United States tourists. They enter Canada at various border points across the country and travel across the country spending their money at motels, gasoline stations and on other services until they arrive at Port McNicoll. There they can park their cars and go by boat to Fort William and Port Arthur at the head of the lakes. The cost of the fare is approximately $100 per person. For another $25 they can put their car on the boat. The boat carries roughly 200 passengers plus freight, as I have already said. The two boats, the Keewatin and the Assinihoia, sail and carry passengers for approximately 10 weeks of the year and they are fully booked throughout
[Mr, Berger,!

the year. In other words, if you do not get your ticket and your berth at the beginning of the season you are not going to get on either boat.
Ever since the Noronic fire in Toronto there has been a stepping up in the precautions which should be taken to prevent fire on boats. As you will recall, Mr. Speaker, in the case of the Noronic the passengers slept on the boat. I want to make it perfectly clear, in the case of the Assiniboia and the Keewatin, that when they are in port the passengers do not stay on board; they must leave the ship. I also want to make it perfectly clear that they have the best sprinkler system and the best equipment which can be purchased, as well as lifeboats. The problem is that they were both built in the days of wood. Many of the things on them today do not come up to present day requirements.
My feeling is this. Millions of dollars are being spent by tourists travelling on these boats. I have known people who take these boats, proceed right through to British Columbia by car and then come back to board the boat again at Fort William or Port Arthur to return to Port McNicoll, finally making their way to their border crossing point. Many of them repeat these trips.
We are badly in need of United States dollars. Visitors from the United States spend about $500 million in Canada, money which we badly need owing to our deficit which is something in the order of $1.5 billion. A tourist dollar is just as valuable as a dollar earned through selling goods in the United States. Not only that, the market can be an expanding one. The beauties and the charm of the great lakes and the 30,000 islands provide some of the finest scenery anywhere in the world.
I would say to the Minister of Transport that his department should take another look at this order. When the order was issued the C.P.R. said that they were going to discontinue the service. They will still keep the Assiniboia carrying freight. The Keewatin will be sold if they can sell her. Recently representatives of one of the Caribbean countries or islands were in Canada looking at this boat with the idea of purchasing it. The Department of Transport must take another look at this matter and not lose the tourist dollars which are so valuable to us. This is one of the best tourist drawing cards I know of across Canada. Let us take another look at the equipment of this boat and consider the fact that passengers do not remain on the

If this cannot be done the government should buy the boats and give them to the Canadian National Railway to run. I do not know how many members realize it but these are the last two passenger boats Canada has on the great lakes. I for one feel we should have enough pride in this country not to let this great tourist attraction die especially as it brings so much money to Canada. I should like now to draw the attention of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill), or one of the other ministers in his absence, to the fact that in the Trent waterway system we have one of the finest fresh waterways in the world. To complete this waterway in 1919 two marine railways were built. One of them still operates. They were built as a quick means to get power in the first great war and the marine railways were put in there as a make-do device. Today we still have one of them. It was not until many years after they were built that the Conservative government decided in 1960 to go ahead and rebuild and repair the whole of the Trent waterway system at an expenditure of some $12 million. We believe this will run to $20 million later. In my view this was and is a worthwhile expenditure. Today if you go to this region and travel there you will see that the lift locks at Peterborough have been repaired. You will see also the repairs under way at
January 27, 1966

The Address-Mr. Rynard Kirkfield. You will go up to the Severn river and there you will find one of the finest locks in the world. It was started by the Conservative government and it was opened last year.
The whole morale of the employees of the Trent waterway system was raised by what that Conservative government achieved and by what the present government has been carrying on. The men on the locks have uniforms and caps. The United States tourist knows whom to address. It is a pleasing state of affairs compared with the rundown condition that existed over 22 years of later Liberal administration, five years of Conservative government and the period of the previous Liberal administration from 1919 on.
There is one stumbling block. There is another lock to go in. There is another marine railway which is closed to all intents and purposes to the big boats that come up the waterway. Before the recess I had pointed out the heavy responsibility that rests on the members of this house, particularly of the two older parties, to insure that parliament functions. I feel that the heaviest responsibility of all rests on the government, and it is up to the government to decide how effectively this parliament will operate. The government should recognize that the voters of Canada have had enough of party politics just for the sake of politics. They want parliament to get on with the job. In order to insure that we can get on with the job ahead of us, the government must free itself from its archaic attitude toward what constitutes a motion of non-confidence. It must recognize the right of the opposition to express itself on matters of opinion.

When I refer to the opposition, I could make the same suggestion about the backbenchers on the government side who would love an opportunity to express their opinions without being told that they must vote for the government on any occasion. We must be able to express an opinion without threats which seek to establish that an adverse expression of opinion constitutes a call for an election. This attitude of the government to which I refer is an attitude of playing Russian roulette; it is an attitude that will keep this house in a constant state of election alertness. Every vote in this house could become a cliff-hanger, and sooner or later this government may fall by accident. Then the government will have no one to blame but itself.
A good example of the kind of thing we can expect is the amendment that has been moved by the Conservative party and will be voted upon tonight. This afternoon the New Democratic party released a statement to the press, which I should like to read into the record:
The New Democratic party re-emphasizes its position that amendments to the Speech from the Throne do not constitute non-confidence motions unless they specifically say so. We do not intend to allow the government to blackmail us into silence by the constant threat of an election. Neither do we intend to allow the Conservatives to manoeuvre us into a constant bear-baiting of the government by the moving of phony amendments.
The amendment moved by the official opposition savours more of harassment than an attempt to deal with a matter which properly belongs to this debate. It is obvious that the sales tax is a matter for the budget where it can be considered in conjunction with all other tax proposals. The New Democrats believe now, as we argued in the last parliament, that the government should seek an early opportunity to remove the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials as an incentive to home construction and we intend to urge this in the budget debate.
However, the amendment now before the house seems to us to be an attempt to keep the political pot boiling without any constructive purpose. As we have shown already, we are prepared to support or move amendments calling upon the house to express its views on major issues of policy but we do not favour using this privilege for the purpose of pointless harassment. We will not hesitate to register our views on the substance of this amendment at the appropriate time but we have no intention of being manoeuvred into helping those transparently seeking to keep parliament in a continual state of ferment at a time when there is so much to be done.
This is a time for constructive proposals and legislative action but not for playing games with parliament. In our opinion the amendment proposed by the Conservatives seems to have no basis other than political gamesmanship and we shall therefore vote against it.

Mr. Speaker, along with the other members of this house who have spoken thus far, I should like to congratulate you not only upon your nomination as Speaker of this house, but also for the way in which you have conducted the business of the house so far. I am pleased to have this opportunity to sit in the twenty seventh parliament as the member for Renfrew North. My constituency is a rather large one from a geographical point of view, stretching some six miles north from the town of Renfrew along the Ottawa river to within four miles of Mattawa. It is bordered on the south and west by Renfrew South and part of the Algonquin park. In the north it borders the riding of Nipissing. The southern end of the riding is largely a farming community, forest products playing a big role in the economy of the remainder of the riding. The upper Ottawa valley in general has not prospered during the recent economic boom in Canada to the extent that would even begin to compare with certain other areas in Canada. Promotion of industry and incentives to encourage industries are needed urgently if the upper Ottawa valley is going to grow and expand in the years to come. We are fortunate in having the military camp at Petawawa, the Atomic Energy plant at Chalk River, the townsite of Deep River, Dominion Magnesium and Light Alloy at Haley Station, Steel Equipment Limited, Canada Veneer and other wood industries to provide employment and strength for the community at Pembroke.

The Ottawa river was for many years the canoe route of Indian tribes, cou-reurs de bois and other fur traders. Samuel de Champlain visited the area now known as Renfrew North in the year 1613. It was in that year that he lost his astrolabe, an instrument for measuring latitude and longitude, near the village of Cobden and it was turned up on the shore of Green lake by a farm hand in 1867. Like many other of our famous Canadian relics and souvenirs, it has found its way to a museum in New York city. In that same year he visited Morrison's island in the Ottawa river, three miles from Pembroke. Early Canadians recognized the Ottawa route as the gateway to the north. Jean Talon recognized the Ottawa as the key to northern development of the fur trade.
Today we are faced with a shortage of water in our great lakes system. There have been many plans put forth for the replenishment of the great lakes but to date the great replenishment and northern development concept better known as the Grand Canal is the

January 27, 1966

The Address-Mr. Hopkins only proposal which protects the Canadian water heritage by recycling, not by diverting, northern rivers. By its very name the basic goal of the Grand Canal lies in linking the major, multiple, and urgent water services needs of the mid-continent to the important long term development needs of Canada's north, and its vast water resources. Further, it would do this important job for the profit of all concerned and with the full protection, in perpetuity, of Canada's water heritage as its foundation stone. The plan calls for a large dam across the lower part of James Bay. Behind this dam the fresh water from the Ontario and Quebec rivers flowing into the lower end of James bay would be collected. This water would then be pumped up the Harricanaw river by means of a series of pumping stations equipped with locks. The lift over the height of land would be approximately 950 feet. The water would then be transferred southward through a series of locks to the lake Temiscamingue system and hence into the Ottawa river.
This concept proposes to pump water up the Mattawa river, into Trout lake and then into lake Nipissing, the French river and hence into Georgian bay and the great lakes. Not only does this idea provide for the replenishment of the great lakes, but it also provides for Northern development. The eventual plan calls for barge navigation through to James bay. It also calls for ship navigation of the French river, lake Nipissing, the Mattawa river and the Ottawa river route to the St. Lawrence. Thus it would bring back to modern life in a realistic form the historical use of the Ottawa river.
We must also note at this stage that this route is 282 miles shorter from the Lakehead to Montreal than the present great lakes system. Hence, it would cut down on shipping charges for grain. As we advance as an industrial nation the twin locks at Welland will not suffer from the loss of any diverted traffic.
What we must remember is to look ahead. Without a water replenishment system for the great lakes, industry in central Canada could very well be in trouble for a few years. We are already hearing reports that lake Erie is a dying lake. This country cannot afford to have this danger hanging over it, let alone the possibility of reality, if such is the case. The saviour of the Canadian economy is water replenishment of the great lakes, and the salvation of our Canadian culture and identity as a strong nation would seem to be

northern development, of which the navigation and water control of the Ottawa river canal to Georgian bay, and navigational development of the water route to James Bay, are integral and necessary parts. We seem to be prone to move farther inland and take up challenges of development. I would also like to point out that such bold steps as these may seem odd, peculiar and hard to realize. But if someone had told us ten years ago that man was going to fly to the moon we would have sneered. Today it is within the realm of possibility.
The Fathers of Confederation did not pick Ottawa as a capital just because it was an inland town. They chose it also because it was on a main water route. Today we have time to act in such a way that provincial rights under the British North America Act would be protected. A royal commission could be appointed to investigate the feasibility of the entire Grand Canal project. If we wait until a crisis arises, then stronger action will be necessary and this strong direction would of necessity have to come from the federal government, and use of the elastic clause in the British North America Act may have to be called into play.

It should have the power to hire other competent people as the need arises.

The Grand Canal provides the answers to these problems, as well as providing the key for progress in eastern and northern Ontario, western and northern Quebec, and other parts of Canada on the great lakes system. This type of development will provide economic stability and, with economic stability, history has taught us that we will have a strong, united nation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the matter which I wish to raise at this time arises out of a question put to the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury) on orders of the day regarding the United States auto pact and, in particular, the alleged loss of millions of dollars that is taking place as a result of the proposed cancellation of certain orders of metal stamping companies engaged in the industry.
We raised with the minister today the very genuine fears being expressed by United Auto Workers and their legitimate requests for a tripartite meeting amongst the unions, the minister and the industry involved. As has been the case throughout the history of this agreement, this request has been arrogantly brushed aside by the minister. In my judgment this corresponds with his attitude since the inception of the pact.
When this matter first came before us, we could not get any information. We finally had to write to the United States to get sufficient information. We were unable to get proper answers from the minister. We were unable to have the matter go to a committee where it could be studied. We were merely told that in their almighty judgment they knew what was right.
The minister will recall that we tried to have adjustment assistance for dislocation. Dislocation was denied; but it subsequently took place and a sort of piecemeal plan was introduced. We now have another problem arising out of this agreement, which has been shrouded in mystery since its inception, and that is the dislocation which has resulted to these metal stamping companies.
Once again the trade unions involved are having difficulties which arise out of decisions made by this government in its negotiations between the United States and the manufacturing companies. We think that the rights of the workers ought to be taken into consideration.
[Mr. DiefenbakerJ
I plead with the minister, as I did before, to stop his arrogant treatment of this agreement in this house, his brushing aside of any suggestions put forward by the opposition, his brushing aside of the requests made by the workers involved. They have a big stake in this agreement. They want to partake of it. They want consultation. They do not want to be told that what the government has decided is in their best interests. This has been the history of this agreement throughout.
The minister said this morning that he did not think a tripartite meeting would be useful. I should like to know why. When would one be useful? Why has this very legitimate request of the trade union involved been denied?

Mr. Speaker, French speaking members of the union are complaining that they cannot submit their grievances to the appeal board of the union because all the proceedings take place in English and therefore representations of the French speaking members could not be heard. Since French speaking members cannot understand or speak English, they are therefore deprived of a fundamental right, namely to be heard in their mother tongue by the committee which must pass judgment on them.
This very morning, I tried to obtain from the minister the assurance that he would see that those allegations are substantiated and inform the House of the corrective measures he intends to take in order to remedy a really deplorable situation, if it actually exists, and which is seriously detrimental to all members of that union who are awaiting a decision of this appeal board return to their jobs if such would be the case.
I should also like to take this opportunity to call the attention of the Minister of Labour, responsible for the trusteeship of this union, to a seemingly obvious anomaly, if one examines the list of members of this appeal
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion board of the Seafarers' International Union: three of the members sitting on this appeal board are apparently members of the executive council of the union.
Since members often have to air grievances which may involve the authorities, that is to say the officers of this union, I believe there is, on that point, an anomaly through which the aggrieved party is deprived of his opportunity to submit his grievances objectively and so to have them objectively and loyally considered by the members of the appeal board.
I ask the minister to investigate this matter which I consider very serious; indeed, last August, that is, on the 25th of August 1965, Mr. Michel de la Chevrotiere who was a member of the appeal committee of the Seafarers' International Union, had to resign because he could neither understand nor speak English. In view of the fact that the evidence is given, and the questioning takes place, in English only, I feel this is surely a flagrant injustice which should be redressed.
Such is the situation within that union.
I ask the minister to take immediate steps to ensure that these people who have been or may be wronged by such an anomaly obtain justice and to inform the House at an early date what measures the government intends to take to give justice to these members of the Seafarers' International Union.
